occurrences.description: North Richmond Street, being blind, is quiet except when the Christian Brothers' School sets the boys free; an uninhabited house stands at the blind end and the other houses gaze at one another with brown imperturbable faces.
The former tenant of the house, a priest, died in the back drawing-room; in his will he left his money to institutions and his furniture to his sister.
In the waste room behind the kitchen the boy finds a few paper-covered books: The Abbot, The Devout Communicant and The Memoirs of Vidocq; he likes the last best because its leaves are yellow.
In the wild garden behind the house, under a straggling bush, the boy finds the late tenant's rusty bicycle-pump.

In the short days of winter the boys play in the street after dusk until their bodies glow, running through dark muddy lanes past the rough tribes from the cottages, the ashpits and the dark odorous stables.
If the uncle is seen turning the corner, the boys hide in the shadow until they have seen him safely housed.
When Mangan's sister comes out on the doorstep to call her brother in to his tea, the boys watch her from their shadow peer up and down the street.

While her brother teases her before obeying, the boy stands by the railings looking at her; her dress swings as she moves and the soft rope of her hair tosses from side to side, her figure defined by the light from the half-opened door.
Every morning the boy lies on the floor in the front parlour watching her door, the blind pulled down to within an inch of the sash so that he cannot be seen.

When she comes out, the boy seizes his books and follows her, keeping her brown figure always in his eye; near the point where their ways diverge he quickens his pace and passes her. This happens morning after morning; he has never spoken to her except for a few casual words.

On Saturday evenings the boy carries parcels for his aunt through the flaring streets, jostled by drunken men and bargaining women, amid curses of labourers, shrill litanies of shop-boys and the nasal chanting of street-singers.
Amid the market noises the boy imagines that he bears his chalice safely through a throng of foes; her name springs to his lips in strange prayers and praises which he himself does not understand.

The boy's eyes are often full of tears, he cannot tell why, and at times a flood from his heart seems to pour itself out into his bosom; his body is like a harp and her words and gestures like fingers running upon the wires.

One dark rainy evening the boy goes into the back drawing-room where the priest died; hearing rain on the sodden beds through a broken pane, he presses his palms together until they tremble, murmuring 'O love! O love!' many times.
At last she speaks to him, asking was he going to Araby; he forgets whether he answered yes or no. It would be a splendid bazaar, she says; she would love to go.
The boy asks her, 'And why can't you?'

While she speaks she turns a silver bracelet round and round her wrist; she cannot go because there will be a retreat that week in her convent. Her brother and two other boys are fighting for their caps and the boy is alone at the railings.

She holds one of the spikes, bowing her head towards him; the light from the lamp opposite catches the white curve of her neck, lights up her hair and the hand upon the railing, and catches the white border of a petticoat, just visible as she stands at ease.
She says, 'It's well for you.'
The boy says, 'If I go, I will bring you something.'

After that evening the boy wishes to annihilate the tedious intervening days; her image comes between him and the page he strives to read, and the syllables of the word Araby are called to him through the silence.
The boy asks for leave to go to the bazaar on Saturday night; his aunt is surprised and hopes it is not some Freemason affair.
The boy answers few questions in class; he watches his master's face pass from amiability to sternness, the master hoping he is not beginning to idle.
On Saturday morning the boy reminds his uncle that he wishes to go to the bazaar in the evening; the uncle, fussing at the hallstand for the hat-brush, answers curtly: 'Yes, boy, I know.'
Unable to lie at the parlour window because the uncle is in the hall, the boy leaves the house in bad humour and walks slowly towards the school through pitilessly raw air.

The uncle not yet home at dinner, the boy mounts to the high cold empty gloomy rooms of the upper house and goes from room to room singing; from the front window he watches his companions playing below and looks over at the dark house where she lives, seeing the brown-clad figure cast by his imagination.

Downstairs the boy finds Mrs Mercer, an old garrulous pawnbroker's widow who collects used stamps for some pious purpose, sitting at the fire; he endures the gossip of the tea-table, the meal prolonged beyond an hour, and still the uncle does not come.

Mrs Mercer stands up to go after eight o'clock, sorry she cannot wait, as the night air is bad for her; the boy begins to walk up and down the room, clenching his fists, and his aunt says, 'I'm afraid you may put off your bazaar for this night of Our Lord.'
At nine o'clock the boy hears his uncle's latchkey in the halldoor, hears him talking to himself and the hallstand rocking under the weight of his overcoat; the boy can interpret these signs.
Midway through his dinner the boy asks the uncle for the money to go to the bazaar; the uncle has forgotten, and says, 'The people are in bed and after their first sleep now.'
The boy does not smile; his aunt says energetically, 'Can't you give him the money and let him go? You've kept him late enough as it is.'

The uncle says he is very sorry he forgot and that he believes in the old saying 'All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy'; told a second time where the boy is going, he asks did he know 'The Arab's Farewell to his Steed' and, as the boy leaves the kitchen, is about to recite its opening lines to the aunt.
The boy holds a florin tightly in his hand as he strides down Buckingham Street towards the station; the streets thronged with buyers and glaring with gas recall to him the purpose of his journey.

The boy takes his seat in a third-class carriage of a deserted train, which after an intolerable delay creeps out among ruinous houses and over the twinkling river; at Westland Row porters keep a crowd back, saying it is a special train for the bazaar, and he remains alone in the bare carriage.

The train draws up beside an improvised wooden platform; the boy passes out onto the road, sees by a lighted clock-dial that it is ten minutes to ten, and before him a large building displays the magical name.
Finding no sixpenny entrance and fearing the bazaar will close, the boy passes in quickly through a turnstile, handing a shilling to a weary-looking man.

The boy finds himself in a big hall girdled at half its height by a gallery; nearly all the stalls are closed, the greater part of the hall is in darkness, and he recognises a silence like that which pervades a church after a service.
Before a curtain over which the words Café Chantant are written in coloured lamps, two men count money on a salver; the boy listens to the fall of the coins.
Remembering with difficulty why he had come, the boy goes over to one of the open stalls and examines porcelain vases and flowered tea-sets.

At the door of the stall a young lady is talking and laughing with two young gentlemen; the boy remarks their English accents and listens vaguely to their conversation, which ends 'O, there's a ... fib!'
Observing him, the young lady comes over and asks did he wish to buy anything; the tone of her voice is not encouraging, as if she has spoken out of a sense of duty.
Looking humbly at the great jars that stand like eastern guards at either side of the dark entrance to the stall, the boy murmurs, 'No, thank you.'
The young lady changes the position of one of the vases and goes back to the two young men; they talk of the same subject, and once or twice she glances at the boy over her shoulder.

The boy lingers before the stall though he knows his stay is useless, then turns away slowly and walks down the middle of the bazaar, allowing the two pennies to fall against the sixpence in his pocket.
A voice calls from one end of the gallery that the light is out; the upper part of the hall is now completely dark.
Gazing up into the darkness the boy sees himself as a creature driven and derided by vanity, and his eyes burn with anguish and anger.
